newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OPEC eyes quota freeze, oil prices rise.
newsitem.headline: OPEC eyes quota freeze, oil prices rise.

text.p: The oil market Wednesday gave OPEC ministers meeting in Vienna an approving nod as the cartel appeared set to hold the line on oil exports for the next six months.

Crude oil was up 18 cents at $23.80 a barrel in early afternoon on the New York Mercantile Exchange, while in London, oil hovered at $22.80 a barrel, compared with only $18 back in June when OPEC last met.

Ministers said the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries needed to exercise caution in setting 1997 production levels, amid doubts on how winter weather may affect heating oil demand and on the timing and volume of resumed Iraqi exports.
Iraq's chief delegate, Osama al-Hiti, told reporters he now expected that Baghdad would start selling oil under a relaxed U.N. Gulf War embargo in "a matter of weeks."
Delegates said OPEC linchpin Saudia Arabia favoured a quota freeze at 25.03 million barrels a day -- despite violations by some of the 11 members -- at least to the end of June.

Ministers who told reporters they favour a "rollover" included Iran's Gholamreza Aqazadeh. He said he would support a 12-month freeze, although Algeria's Amar Makhloufi said he thought that the consensus was for six months.
A brief plenary session of the 101st OPEC ministerial adjourned Wednesday and was to reconvene Thursday when substantive discussion of quotas will begin. Ministers say the talks may end on Thursday.

"OPEC is meeting against a backdrop that can only bring a smile to their lips," said Peter Gignoux, head of the London energy desk at Smith Barney. "Oil is up five dollars. That is in itself an incentive to preserve the status quo."
Prices are strong in spite of both a revived prospect that the 1990 Gulf War ban on Iraqi exports may soon be relaxed and OPEC's own quota violations.
Alleged excess is said by Western monitors to have already propelled OPEC sales by 1 million barrels a day above the 25.03 million ceiling, even before Iraq starts to export 800,000 barrels a day.
Delegates said Saudi Arabia believed the market can absorb more oil, because inventories are low and as a result of the delay so far on resumed Iraqi sales.
Iraq this week agreed to U.N. conditions that had held up implementing an oil-for-food pact to let it sell $2 billion worth of oil to help buy food and medicine.

Iraq's al-Hiti said in Vienna that only a pricing formula and "very minor technicalities" had now to be ironed out. He said Iraq expected to export 700,000 to 800,000 barrels daily using up in full the country's OPEC quota allocation.
Depending on its severity, the winter can swing oil demand by a million barrels daily, Barclays Bank economists said in their latest Commodities Survey.
Barclays has revised up its forecast for average 1996 oil prices to $20 per barrel from only $16.80 in 1995. But they noted that "our view remains that prices are likely to ease next year."

The expectation that prices will be weaker by perhaps $1 a barrel is based on the "strong possibility" of revived Iraqi exports and a prospect of increased supply from the North Sea, Asia and Latin America.
